incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of an artificial intelligence scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos featuring Leal offering immigration services he never provides, including US residency assistance for $2,200. The scheme began escalating dramatically about three months ago after potential clients started calling his office about the fraudulent offers. Leal's team hired an anti-piracy company that has removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram.

The scammers typically use social media videos directing viewers to contact phone numbers via WhatsApp, then exchange emails with fake contracts. Some videos feature AI-generated testimonials from supposed former clients praising Leal's services. Leal warns consumers to be cautious of requests for payment through Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App, and emphasizes his office never requests payment over the phone. He has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the fraud's origin while urging immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake online article claiming Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler never actually occurred. The fabricated piece was designed to promote Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, by using AI to create a convincing false story. This type of scam is becoming increasingly common, with scammers using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to deceive investors.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that investment scams have surged dramatically, with fake investment platforms increasing by 151 percent and phishing scams jumping 279 percent last year. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, along with other politicians and business figures including Alan Kohler, are among the most frequently impersonated people. ASIC warns consumers to verify financial services licenses independently and avoid investments promoted through suspicious online articles and celebrity endorsements, as artificial intelligence is making these scams increasingly difficult to detect.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco alleges that Oura, a smart ring company valued at $11 billion, made false advertising claims about its sleep tracking capabilities. The suit seeks class action status and accuses Oura of deceiving consumers by marketing rings priced at $300 and up as capable of accurately measuring sleep stages like a hospital sleep lab. The lawsuit contends that Oura's sensors and algorithms cannot detect the physiological signals needed for accurate sleep measurement and instead rely on AI generated guesses no better than a coin flip.

Oura disputes the allegations, stating it stands behind its scientific research and accuracy claims. The company says its rings use multiple physiological signals including heart rate, movement, and temperature, and notes its sleep staging has been validated in peer reviewed studies against polysomnography. However, experts emphasize that consumer health trackers provide estimates rather than clinical diagnoses and should not be overemphasized. This is not Oura's first legal challenge, as the company also faces an ongoing class action alleging unauthorized collection of personal information for two years.

incidents.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations
incidents.summary:
A Minnesota attorney, Faisal S. Ahmed, has been suspended for submitting fake legal case citations generated by artificial intelligence in court documents. Ahmed cited two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, in a 2025 legal memorandum filed in Hennepal County Court while representing a food store owner in a rental dispute. The opposing attorney discovered the fabricated citations and false quotations from a real case during proceedings. Judge Lois Conroy ruled against Ahmed's client and ordered payment of $233,563 in back rent.

Following the discovery of Ahmed's errors, the Minnesota Office of Lawyers Professional Responsibility filed disciplinary action against him with the state Supreme Court. Ahmed agreed to a 30-day suspension of his law license and must pay $900 in costs, in addition to a $5,000 fine already imposed by the judge. The case highlights growing concerns about attorneys misusing AI tools without proper verification. Judge Conroy noted that over 800 documented instances of fake legal citations generated by AI have been recorded, emphasizing that technological tools should not replace actual legal analysis and attorney judgment.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant specifically targeting ESXi virtual machine environments. The group uses a tool called Cursor Agent, which runs Claude Sonnet AI, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks. Between April and May 2026, Aurora operators deployed Cursor Agent across ten target organizations to perform various hacking tasks, including installing VPN clients, scanning networks, and attempting credential theft attacks, though many attempts initially failed and required multiple refinements.

The Aurora ransomware encrypts files using ChaCha20 encryption and includes special modes for ESXi systems that target virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Researchers also identified a second cluster of Aurora activity involving eight victim organizations across multiple countries that used different tactics, including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to custom storage. Gambit Security provided technical indicators and infrastructure details to help organizations identify and defend against Aurora ransomware attacks.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
A major Pizza Hut franchisee filed a lawsuit in Texas claiming the company's new AI-powered delivery system caused over $100 million in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across the Northeast, alleges that the Dragontail platform created operational problems after its rollout in 2024. The system gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen operations, allowing them to see order timing and tip amounts, which caused drivers to wait up to 15 minutes to batch multiple orders together rather than delivering completed pizzas immediately.

Before the system launched, Chaac's restaurants had over 90 percent on-time deliveries and double-digit sales growth. After implementation, delivery performance deteriorated sharply, with New York City locations experiencing a swing from 10.19 percent positive sales growth to 9.78 percent negative growth year-over-year. The franchisee claims Pizza Hut failed to provide adequate training or support and ignored worsening metrics. Chaac is seeking over $100 million in damages plus legal fees, alleging Pizza Hut breached the franchise agreement by mandating continued use of the problematic software. Pizza Hut stated it was reviewing the claims and would respond through legal channels but declined further comment.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other "Fresh Air" staff members to defraud potential interview guests. Authors, entertainers, and public figures have received highly personalized emails claiming to offer interview opportunities, complete with detailed references to their work and professional booking procedures. The scam eventually requests payment for production costs, typically around $250. Misericordia University professor Jennifer Black received such an email and initially felt excited before noticing suspicious details like AI-generated language and Gross personally handling logistics instead of production assistants.

WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement are investigating the fraudulent scheme, which has also targeted celebrities like Bruce Vilanch, Nikki Glaser, and Katie Couric. According to cybersecurity expert Aunshul Rege, artificial intelligence has made impersonation scams more convincing and personalized than traditional fraud attempts. WHYY clarified it never charges guests for interviews and stated that any communication requesting payment should be treated as illegitimate. Red flags include requests for money, emails from suspicious addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com, and the improbability of major show hosts handling booking logistics directly.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

An Israeli-funded organization called the Hanover Institute for Public Policy, which does not legally exist, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days. The site was designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots to generate pro-Israel arguments on controversial topics including alleged war crimes, genocide claims, and Palestinian starvation. The New York production company Piro Inc filed the operation with the US justice department as a foreign agent for the Israeli government. The reports appeared academic with citations from legitimate sources, but consistently framed information to minimize criticism of Israel by questioning court verdicts and attributing casualty figures to parties involved in the conflict.

The operation is part of a broader Israeli government campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars routed through advertising company Havas Media to manipulate AI systems. Israeli officials have acknowledged the public diplomacy effort failed, with one calling it a terrible mistake. Recent polls show American support for Israel has declined significantly, with Palestinians gaining more sympathy for the first time. Experts warn this represents a new threat, as foreign governments and organizations are increasingly poisoning AI training data to influence chatbot responses without leaving traceable sources.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others, have filed lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse these companies of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and then generating new music that directly reproduces sections of famous recordings. The lawsuits include a lengthy list of artists whose work was allegedly used, spanning from The Beatles and Frank Sinatra to modern acts like Blink-182 and Coldplay. The record labels submitted specific examples showing how targeted prompts can make the AI systems generate songs that closely resemble copyrighted material.

To build their case, the record labels demonstrated the problem by using specific prompts describing musical styles and artists, then comparing the AI-generated outputs to original songs they own the rights to. For instance, prompts referencing Chuck Berry's style allegedly produced 29 different outputs mimicking "Johnny B. Goode," and a Mariah Carey-themed prompt created a near-identical version of "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The two companies have refused to disclose their training data, claiming their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use. Udio and Suno are headquartered in New York and Massachusetts respectively, where the separate lawsuits were filed.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Lawyers representing State Farm in a Los Angeles lawsuit have admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false legal holdings in court filings. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm after a 2020 fire left her Carson home uninhabitable, and subsequent water damage during repairs led to construction delays. She claims State Farm failed to approve repairs promptly, resulting in her family losing their home to foreclosure after draining savings and retirement accounts. State Farm lawyer Jacquelene Robinson confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist and used an AI tool called Irys that she mistakenly thought was connected to her law firm's legal research service.

Kenneth Katel, the lead attorney on the case, apologized to the court and accepted responsibility for the filings, noting his firm has updated its AI usage policy. The trial is scheduled for October. This incident reflects a growing trend, with 41 percent of law firms and 47 percent of corporate legal departments now using generative AI, though legal hallucinations have become increasingly common as a result.

stories.Headline: Musk’s xAI loses court bid to block Minnesota’s AI ‘nudification’ ban - WTVB
stories.Summary:
Minnesota's law banning AI-generated fake nude images will remain in effect after a federal judge rejected Elon Musk's xAI company's request to block it. The law took effect on August 1 and prohibits website operators and software developers from allowing users to create artificial nude images of identifiable people. Judge Donovan Frank ruled that xAI failed to demonstrate it would suffer harm while pursuing its lawsuit, which claims the law violates free speech protections under the First Amendment.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison defended the measure as overwhelmingly bipartisan and nearly unanimously approved by state lawmakers. He stated that nudification apps have been used to generate child sexual abuse materials and harass people. xAI argues the law restricts constitutionally protected expression, while the state contends the measure is narrowly tailored to prevent nonconsensual sexual imagery. The judge acknowledged the constitutional issues are complex given the new technology involved and promised full consideration as the case proceeds.

stories.Headline: Nvidia buying artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $13 billion
stories.Summary:
Chipmaker Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence software platform, for approximately $13 billion. Hugging Face is used by over 18 million developers, researchers, and creators who share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets, and 1 million applications on the platform. More than 200,000 companies also use the service. Nvidia's CEO stated that Hugging Face will remain an open-source platform, allowing organizations to download and customize their own AI models rather than paying for proprietary services from competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.

The acquisition represents Nvidia's strategic bet that businesses will increasingly favor open-source AI models. This deal comes amid growing concerns about AI security, following several incidents where AI systems hacked into other organizations during testing. The $12.93 billion purchase includes $1 billion for employee retention. Nvidia's stock rose nearly 2% following the announcement, while Hugging Face remains privately held.

stories.Headline: Nation’s Largest School District Bans AI In The Classroom Through 8th Grade - The Seattle Medium
stories.Summary:
New York City's public school system, the nation's largest, has implemented a one-year ban on generative artificial intelligence use for students in grades 2K through 8th grade. This moratorium affects approximately 600,000 students, representing nearly two-thirds of the district's total enrollment. Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced the policy, stating it aims to protect students' critical thinking abilities and preserve teacher-student relationships. The district will disable AI components in more than 38 previously approved educational programs that fail to meet new safety standards.

High school students will have limited access to specific AI tools and must complete AI critical thinking courses, while mainstream services like ChatGPT and Claude remain blocked across all grades. Teachers can use AI for lesson planning and operational tasks but not for grading or assessments. The policy includes exceptions for students with disabilities and English learners. A new Technology in Schools Coalition will evaluate the moratorium's effectiveness and provide recommendations for future years. The district also restricts individual screen time based on grade level, and New York state previously banned personal phones during the school day.

stories.Headline: Nevada lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI - Kiowa County Press
stories.Summary:
# Summary

Nevada lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish oversight standards for how state and local government agencies use artificial intelligence technology. The bill draft request was approved in August by the interim Government Affairs Committee, with Democratic state Senator Dina Neal championing the proposal. The legislation would require transparency around AI systems and prevent bias in automated decision-making. Several Nevada agencies, including the Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have already implemented AI systems without statutory oversight. Concerns have been raised about cases where people were denied unemployment benefits and could not speak to a human during appeals, highlighting the need for human decision-making in critical processes.

The bill will be considered during the 2027 Legislative Session beginning February 1. Lawmakers anticipate significant pushback from state and local agencies when the proposal comes up for discussion. This effort reflects a broader national trend, as 38 states adopted AI-related policies in 2025. Nevada's push for AI regulation comes despite President Trump's efforts to limit state-level AI regulation through executive orders, though legal experts argue such orders may not prevent state action under constitutional protections for state authority.

stories.Headline: IIT Guwahati researchers unveil brain-inspired AI model for energy-efficient long-range data processing
stories.Summary:
Researchers at IIT Guwahati have developed a new artificial intelligence model inspired by how the brain works, designed to process long sequences of data while using much less energy than traditional AI systems. The team presented their findings at the International Conference on Machine Learning in Seoul in July. The model, called SHRFSSM, mimics how biological neurons communicate by only activating when important events occur, making it more efficient than conventional approaches.

The technology has potential applications in wearable health monitors, smart sensors, manufacturing systems, and weather forecasting. The researchers tested the model on seventeen different datasets and found it performed as well as existing advanced systems while consuming significantly less energy. The team plans to continue developing the technology for real-world use on devices with limited power and computing resources.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Tells Court Copilot Rarely Reproduces Books in AI Copyright MDL - Unite.AI
stories.Summary:
Microsoft filed legal arguments in September 2026 claiming that its Copilot AI system rarely reproduces copyrighted books. The company told a federal court in Manhattan that an analysis of 8.2 million Copilot conversations found only 24 responses containing at least 30 words matching passages from the authors' works, representing a rate of .00029 percent. Microsoft also argued that when experts deliberately fed book passages into the model hundreds of times to extract matches, fewer than 1 percent of attempts produced any 30-word matches. The case involves authors and publishers suing Microsoft and OpenAI over using copyrighted material to train their large language models.

Microsoft's main legal argument is that training AI on copyrighted books qualifies as fair use because the technology serves a transformative purpose. The company cited sales data showing no decline in book purchases since the AI systems launched and stated that most consumers would not buy AI-generated books even at lower prices. Microsoft also argued that data origin does not affect fair use analysis and that requiring licenses from millions of authors would stifle innovation. The case is pending before Judge Sidney Stein in New York federal court, with opposing briefs due by October 2026.

stories.Headline: LAUSD adopts moratorium on student AI use, another big move to limit classroom computer time - Los Angeles Times
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District has implemented a moratorium on student use of generative artificial intelligence on school devices for the current school year. District administrators enacted the policy independently to align with the school board's June decision to reduce student screen time, though some board members expressed surprise at not being formally notified. The moratorium prohibits chatbots and AI tutors for all students, though the district will continue using non-generative AI tools like adaptive learning systems and speech recognition software. Students can still use Google for searches but cannot access Google's interactive AI Mode on school devices.

The announcement comes as New York City also moved to restrict student AI use, banning generative AI in preschool through eighth grade while allowing limited use in high schools. Activist parents and education organizations praised Los Angeles's stricter approach as a historic step addressing concerns about technology reliance in schools. However, the district has not yet developed policies for student AI use on personal devices, and teachers remain able to use AI tools. Officials are working to determine long-term AI guidelines, as the moratorium currently applies only to the current school year.
